title: The turning
hookLine: the whirling ceremony was shaped by Rumi's son Sultan Walad and the Mevlevi order after Rumi's death

cards: Men in tall honey-colored hats and long white skirts, turning and turning, their skirts opened out like bells, heads tilted, one hand raised. You've probably seen the picture, on a travel poster or a phone screen.
People call them whirling dervishes, and they've become almost a logo for Rumi. So, a question worth asking: did Rumi invent that ceremony, the way it's performed in Konya every December?
The honest answer is more interesting than yes.

teach.b: Sema comes from the Arabic sama, which means listening. In Sufi circles it meant gathering to hear music and poetry, and letting the hearing move you, sometimes into movement.

Accounts from Rumi's circle say he turned, and a story people tell has him starting to spin in the bazaar at the rhythm of goldsmiths' hammers. That turning was free, unplanned, part of his grief and joy after Shams.
The ceremony in the photos came later.

After Rumi died in 1273, his student Husam al-Din led the circle for a time, and then his son Sultan Walad gathered the followers and shaped them into an order, the Mevlevis, named after Rumi's title, Mevlana, our master.
Over the following centuries the order gave the turning a set form, with its music, its steps and its meanings. The tall felt hat is often explained as a tombstone. The white skirt, a shroud.
The black cloak dropped at the start, the grave left behind.
The turner begins with arms crossed on the chest, then opens them: the right palm turned up to receive from heaven, the left turned down to pass it on to the earth.
The turning goes around the heart, slowly, calmly, eyes soft.

teach.h: ONE PALM UP, ONE PALM DOWN.
teach.b: It isn't a dance for an audience.
For the Mevlevis it's worship, a prayer done with the whole body, with the reed flute from the Masnavi's opening sounding over it.
In 1925 the new Turkish Republic closed the Sufi orders, and for years the ceremony went quiet. Today it's performed again, and UNESCO has listed it as world heritage.

how: In the Mevlevi order, the sema is a formal act of worship: the turners, called semazens, turn to the ney and drum in a set ceremony, right palm up and left palm down, most well known for it, in Konya each December.

o: the Mevlevi turning, a prayer of listening and movement
a whirling folk dance put on for festival crowds
a set of rules Rumi wrote down for his followers

p: Rumi's son, who shaped the order

s: Rumi designed the ceremony exactly as it's performed today

games.q: Rumi has died. his followers are grieving, and they have his turning and his poems. you're his son. what do you do?
o: gather them into an order around his ways.
write down his rules and close the door.
games.why: Sultan Walad gathered Rumi's followers and shaped the Mevlevi order, which over centuries gave the turning its set form.

practice: Turn slowly once, but only if you have space and feel steady; otherwise stay seated and turn just your gaze around the room.
Stand, cross your arms on your chest and breathe, then very slowly open your hands, one palm up, one palm down, and turn one full circle at the speed of a clock's second hand, eyes soft.
Stop, cross your arms again, and stand still.

wordCard.voice: Sema. From the Arabic for listening: the Mevlevi turning ceremony, shaped after Rumi's death by his son and his order. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: listening; in Sufi use, gathering for music and poetry. Turkish spells it sema.

carryVoice: Your line: turn slowly. One palm to receive, one to pass it on. See you tomorrow.
